entries.label: Tell us how you heard about Zipline and this job!
Are you available for a full-time onsite internship this summer (May/June - August/September)?
Why are you interested in becoming an Enterprise Systems Software Engineering Intern?
entries.value:
The work I keep coming back to is software that sits inside a real operational workflow, where a wrong action has a cost. I built a Playwright job-application agent in TypeScript where every application moves through an explicit state machine and every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED. I also built a validation ladder so a capability is not called working just because it passes against a local fixture. That is the mindset I would bring to internal business systems: state has to live in one place, integrations have to fail safely, and the human has to stay in the loop where judgment matters.

I care about operational usefulness over model novelty. On the anomaly-detection system I work on now, the harder problem was not scoring events but prioritizing and explaining alerts, because a system that produces too many alerts just creates a second problem.

Zipline runs autonomous logistics on four continents with a delivery every 30 seconds. Systems at that scale only work if the internal tooling behind them is reliable, and I want to own real pieces of that rather than isolated tickets.

entries.label: Tell us about a project where something didn’t work as expected. What was the problem and how did you figure out what to do next?
entries.value: The clearest example is my independent research on how scientific work gets funded and evaluated. I started with a strong hypothesis: the main constraints on research were compensation and grant-writing burden. I spent a year reading papers and institutional history, then interviewed researchers, research administrators, economists, and people building alternative research organizations, and the interviews kept contradicting me. Many people were consciously trading compensation for autonomy and task choice, so my explanation did not hold. What I did next was change the question instead of defending the thesis. I now think the bigger effect is selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review, and some ideas never get attempted. I also prototyped thinking around automated reproducibility of papers. It looked technically valuable, but once I asked who would actually pay for a system that surfaces problems in already-published work, the model got much weaker and I stopped pushing it. That pattern has carried into my engineering work: I try to find the assumption that would make the whole thing wrong, test it early, and be willing to drop the version I liked.

entries.label: Describe a recent project where you used AI tools while building software. What did the AI help with, and what parts still required your judgement?
entries.value:
On my job-application agent, I used OpenAI only at narrow call sites rather than letting a model drive the browser. The model helped with parsing and interpreting messy ATS form structures and drafting text, which is the part where language variation is endless and rules break down. Everything else was my judgment encoded in the system: the explicit state machine each application moves through, SQLite as the single source of truth so state cannot diverge across processes, Zod validation at boundaries, and fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED and FORM_FILL_ENABLED that never default on. I also decided that free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled and always generate a human-review item, and that Workday, iCIMS, and Oracle get detected and skipped rather than handled unreliably.

The same split showed up in tSearch, where rubric-driven LLM judges assess dimensions in parallel but cannot re-run discovery or silently fix identity-resolution errors, and missing evidence returns insufficient evidence instead of a low score. AI made generation cheap. Deciding what a system is allowed to act on stayed mine.

entries.label: Tell us about the most technically challenging project you’ve built. What problem were you solving, what decisions did you make, and what would you do differently today?
entries.value:
The hardest thing I've built is the machine-learning core of the anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization system I work on at Summer Atlantic Capital. I own major parts of the data and ML infrastructure: the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and the public detection API. The modeling side is temporal sequence modeling over event streams using RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, and a learning-to-rank layer on top.

The decision that mattered most was treating the real problem as operational rather than statistical. A detector that flags everything just replaces one problem with a worse one, so I put effort into the ranking layer and into an LLM explanation layer built with retrieval-augmented generation so an analyst can see why something was surfaced instead of receiving a bare score. Versioning the service mattered for the same reason: detection behavior changing silently is a failure mode.

What I would do differently is define the alert budget and the evaluation harness with analysts before training anything. I built modeling capability first and then worked backward into what was actually useful, which cost me time.
